question: Reuters recently reported that internal Meta documents estimated that around 10 % of the company’s global revenue for 2024 (about EUR 13.8 billion) would originate from advertising and promoting scams or banned products, with Meta’s platforms displaying approximately 15 billion ‘higher risk’ scam ads per day1.

Such practices appear to generate substantial profit from fraudulent or misleading advertising that also targets European consumers. Given the possible breach of EU consumer protection and unfair commercial practice rules: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the scale of scam advertising affecting EU users on Meta’s platforms, and of any data received from national authorities or the company itself?
Has the Commission assessed Meta revenue linked to such fraudulent ads within the EU market?
Does the Commission intend to examine these practices as potential unfair commercial practices under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive or other relevant EU consumer protection instruments?

Reuters, ‘Meta is earning a fortune on a deluge of fraudulent ads, documents show’, Reuters special report, 6 November 2025, https://www.reuters.com/investigations/meta-is-earning-fortune-deluge-fraudulent-adsdocuments-show-2025-11-06/.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.3.

2026) The Commission is aware of the dissemination of deceptive advertising affecting Facebook and Instagram and is currently investigating these services designated as very large online platforms for potential breaches of the Digital Services Act (DSA)1, particularly regarding the dissemination of deceptive advertisements and coordinated inauthentic behaviour related to financial scams and disinformation.

The Commission cannot comment on the status of ongoing investigations. However, the Commission is engaging with the provider of Facebook and Instagram to gather information regarding any suspected infringement. Under the DSA, that provider is required to supply the requested information relating to the suspected infringement.

The Commission is also engaging with a range of stakeholders on the topic, including civil society organisations and Member State authorities, to gather information to inform the Commission’s work. On 24 October 2025, the Commission addressed preliminary findings to the provider of Facebook and Instagram.

The Commission took the preliminary view that that provider had failed to fulfil, amongst others, its obligations to provide users simple mechanisms to notify illegal content, such as illegal advertisements or offers, as well as to allow them to effectively challenge content moderation decisions in relation to the provision of Facebook and Instagram in the Union2.

The Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) complements specific EU legislation, such as the DSA. It prohibits misleading and aggressive commercial practices when they affect consumer’s transactional decision. The UCPD is transposed into national laws and Member States authorities and courts are responsible for its enforcement.
